opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd frame it carefully. I'm not saying it's provably impossible, but I think it's the hardest wall we're facing, and it may not yield to simply scaling up what we're doing now.

Today's models are extraordinarily good at interpolation. They've absorbed an enormous amount of human-produced text, code, and images, and they can recombine those patterns fluently. But nearly every concept they manipulate was already named, defined, and argued over by people. The model inherits our abstractions. It didn't create them.

Abstracting a genuinely new concept is a different act. Think about the moment someone first formalized "energy," or "information" in Shannon's sense, or "natural selection." Nobody was matching patterns in existing descriptions. They looked at a messy pile of phenomena that nobody had connected and said: there's a single underlying thing here, and it deserves a name and a definition. That requires deciding what to ignore, which distinctions matter, and which similarities are deep rather than superficial. And there's often no training signal telling you you're right. Sometimes it takes decades before the field agrees the concept was useful.

So there are a few reasons I'm skeptical.

First, the objective. These systems are trained to predict and to satisfy what's already in the distribution. A truly new concept is, almost by definition, out of distribution. It can look wrong or meaningless at first. An optimizer rewarded for plausibility is pulled away from exactly the strange leap you need.

Second, grounding. Human abstraction comes out of interacting with the world: experiments that fail, physical intuition, surprise. Our concepts compress experience. A model that mostly sees our descriptions of the world is compressing a compression. It can get very good at that, but it's one step removed from the raw material new ideas come from.

Third, evaluation. Even if a system produced a novel abstraction, how would it know? How would we know? Recognizing a good new concept is itself a deep act of judgment, and right now that judgment is still supplied by humans.

Now, to be fair to the other side: people keep drawing lines in the sand, and AI keeps crossing them. Reinforcement learning, self-play, models running experiments in closed loops: those could change the picture, because they let a system generate its own experience instead of only reading ours. If we ever see an AI propose a concept that reorganizes a field, one humans didn't hand it and then adopt because it's genuinely better, that would be the real milestone. Until then, I think we should be honest that fluency and invention aren't the same thing, and the gap between them may be much wider than the benchmarks suggest.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I'd be careful with the word "insurmountable," but let me explain why I think it's at least the hardest open problem.

Everything these models learn comes from data that already exists. When you train on the whole internet, you're learning the distribution of concepts humans have already named, already written about, already fit into a vocabulary. So the model becomes extremely good at recombining those concepts, interpolating between them, applying them in new contexts. That's genuinely impressive, and it covers a huge fraction of what we call intelligence day to day.

But real abstraction is different. Think about what happened when physicists went from "there's no absolute simultaneity" to actually formulating relativity, or when someone first wrote down the idea of a gene before anyone had seen DNA. The new concept didn't exist in the data. There was no word for it. You had a pile of anomalies, things that didn't fit, and somebody compressed them into a new primitive that made the anomalies disappear. That act of noticing "the existing vocabulary is insufficient" and then inventing a new one, and then having the judgment to know it's a good one, is where I don't see current systems getting traction.

And there's a structural reason. The training objective rewards predicting what comes next in a world described by existing concepts. A genuinely new abstraction, by definition, is low probability under that distribution. The model is being optimized to stay inside the conceptual map, and we're asking it to redraw the map. Scale helps with everything inside the map. It's not obvious scale helps with the boundary.

My own experience in the lab shaped this view. The moment in magic-angle graphene wasn't a calculation. It was staring at data that looked wrong for a long time and slowly realizing that the right frame for it was something we hadn't been using. The hard part wasn't computing. It was knowing which question to ask, and being comfortable sitting in confusion without forcing the data into a known box.

So when I say it may be a barrier, I mean this: we don't currently have a training signal for "invent a concept that doesn't exist yet and is correct." Maybe we'll find one. Maybe interaction with the physical world, running real experiments, provides it. But if we don't, we'll have tools that are brilliant at everything humans already understand, and still dependent on humans for the step that moves understanding forward.

astra-6.text:
I think the difficulty is that learning patterns within an existing conceptual framework and creating a new framework are two different things. When we train an AI, we usually give it a way to represent the world and a criterion for judging whether its answers are good. It can become extremely capable within those conditions. But where does a genuinely new concept come from—one that changes what we represent or even what we consider a good explanation?

For example, you might observe many objects falling and learn to predict their motion. Abstracting a concept like gravity is a further step: you propose something that connects observations that initially seem unrelated. The concept becomes useful because it lets you ask new questions and make predictions beyond the examples you started with.

Now, I wouldn’t say we’ve proved that AI cannot do this. Humans might also form concepts through mechanisms that machines could reproduce. But being able to recombine existing ideas fluently doesn’t, by itself, demonstrate that ability. The difficult question is whether an AI can recognize that its current framework is inadequate, invent a better one, and test it against the world. That’s why I see concept formation as a potentially fundamental barrier, rather than something we can simply assume will disappear with more training data.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the difficulty is that learning an existing concept and creating a new concept are two different things. When we train AI, we’ve already given it a language, a set of categories, and some criterion for what counts as a good answer. It can become extremely good at operating within that framework. But where does the framework itself come from?

A new concept isn’t simply a new combination of words. It gives us a way to recognize a structure we couldn’t clearly describe before. You have to decide which differences matter, which details to ignore, and whether the abstraction actually explains something. Often, that involves interacting with the world and discovering that your existing way of thinking fails.

So the potential barrier is this: if an AI’s learning is confined to the distinctions we’ve already expressed, can it discover a distinction that changes the framework itself? I wouldn’t say we’ve proved that it can’t. But producing fluent explanations of concepts we already understand doesn’t, by itself, demonstrate that ability.
